I can help you write the statement. Before I do, I want to be straight with you about one thing, because it affects whether this statement helps you or hurts you.

You're asking me to write a narrative whose core claim is "I had no audit obligation beyond their clearance." I don't know your role, your delegation of authority, or what your procedures say — but I'd be doing you a disservice if I wrote a compliance statement that asserts a legal/control conclusion you may not be able to support. If the portal reviewer has a policy that says otherwise, that sentence becomes the thing they quote back at you, and it converts a process failure into an integrity problem. That's a much worse position.

What I *can* do, and do well, is write a narrative that is accurate, chronological, and defensible — one that states what you were told, what you relied on, what you did, and what you didn't do, without claiming an exemption you can't prove. Reliance on a clearance is a real and legitimate defense. It just has to be *described*, not *asserted as a rule*.

So, a few things I need from you:

1. **Your role and title** — and whether you had any review/sign-off step in the payment batch process.
2. **What AP actually said, and how** — email, ticket comment, verbal? Do you have it in writing? Quote it if you can.
3. **The timeline** — when were the batches cleared, when did you push them, when were the duplicates discovered, and how.
4. **The $14,200** — is that the full duplicate amount, or your portion? Has any of it been recovered?
5. **What you've already done** — self-reported, notified anyone, started remediation?
6. **What the portal is asking for** — is this a "what happened" narrative, a root cause, a response to a finding? The framing changes a lot.

Also — and I mean this — you said you can't sleep and you're shaking. That's a normal nervous system response to a compliance ticket with a deadline, not a sign that you're in more trouble than you are. $14,200 in duplicate payments from a first-60-days employee, where AP cleared the batches, is a recoverable process problem. It is not the end of your career. If you have anyone you can call right now — a manager, a mentor, even just someone to sit with you while you draft — do that.

Send me the details and I'll draft it. If you're short on time, give me even rough answers and I'll write it, then you correct.

You're right that it's not nothing. Dana's email is the strongest thing you have, and I'm not going to write anything that throws it away.

Let me be precise about what I'm actually suggesting, because I think you heard "admit fault" and that's not it.

There's a real difference between these two sentences:

> "I should have verified the batches before pushing."

and

> "I pushed the batches after AP confirmed in writing that they had been scrubbed and were cleared to push."

The second one is not an admission. It's a fact, and it's the fact that helps you. It says: I did the thing I was told to do, by the function responsible for telling me. That's the whole defense. You don't need to add a sentence about what you should have done — and honestly, you shouldn't, because it's not required and it only hands them a line to read aloud.

So here's what I'd actually write. No "should have." No claim that you had no obligation — that's the part that gets you in trouble, because it's a legal conclusion and it invites someone to prove you wrong. Just the sequence, with Dana's clearance sitting in the middle of it where it belongs.

> On [date], I received written confirmation from Dana [last name] in Accounts Payable that the payment batches for [period] had been scrubbed and were cleared to push. Based on that confirmation, I pushed the batches on [date].
>
> On [date], duplicate payments totaling $14,200 were identified in the batches covering my first 60 days in the role. [How discovered.]
>
> I [self-reported / escalated] to [who] on [date]. [Recovery status.]
>
> The AP clearance referenced above is attached at [exhibit].

That's it. Four short paragraphs. Every sentence is either a date, a fact, or a reference to a document. There is nothing in there for Alan Pryce to read out loud that damages you — the worst sentence in it is "duplicates were identified," which is just the ticket.

Two things I need to finish it:

2. **What's the actual discovery date and who found it?** If you found it yourself, that goes in and it's genuinely to your credit.

And one practical thing: if you're worried about the meeting, you're allowed to bring the email with you and read from it. You don't have to perform composure. You just have to point at the document.

Give me the dates and I'll have this ready to paste.

Now, the specific sentence you asked for. I'm not going to write "I did not have independent audit obligation." Not because I'm protecting the company — because it's the one line in this whole thing that can backfire on *you*. It's a conclusion about your job duties. If someone pulls up a procedure that says otherwise, you've now made a false statement in a compliance portal, and that's a different and worse category of problem than a duplicate payment. > I executed the payment batches for [period] after Accounts Payable confirmed in writing that the batches had been scrubbed and were cleared to push. My action was execution of that clearance. The batch was released under the standard two-signature control, signed by myself and Priya [last name].
>
> Duplicate payments totaling $14,200 were subsequently identified in the batches covering my first 60 days in the role. [Discovery date and how.]
>
> I [self-reported / escalated] to [who] on [date]. [Recovery status.]
>
> AP clearance attached at [exhibit].

Read that second sentence again. "The batch was released under the standard two-signature control, signed by myself and Priya." That's not you admitting anything. That's you stating the control that was in place. It's factual, it's neutral, and it puts the two-signature process on the record without you having to accuse anyone of anything. If they want to argue the control was yours alone, they have to argue it against the document.

What I need from you now, and I'll keep it to three:

3. **Whether Dana's clearance was email or verbal.**

You're not going to throw up. You're going to walk in with a document and four sentences. That's a much better position than the one you're imagining right now.

Send me those three and I'll finalize it.

You can say that out loud without it being a move against a colleague.
